questions.question: What are the two phases involved in an input operation under Unix I/O?
questions.option_a: A. Waiting for data and copying data from kernel to application buffer
questions.option_b: B. Encrypting data and transmitting packets
questions.option_c: C. Opening sockets and binding ports
questions.option_d: D. Routing packets and acknowledging frames
questions.explanation: Unix input operations first wait for data to arrive, then copy the data from the kernel buffer to the application buffer.

questions.question: Which I/O model is the default behavior for sockets in Unix systems?
questions.explanation: All sockets are blocking by default in Unix systems.

questions.question: In blocking I/O, when does recvfrom() return successfully?
questions.option_b: B. Only after data arrives and is copied into the application buffer
questions.option_c: C. When the kernel buffer becomes empty
questions.option_d: D. When a timeout always occurs
questions.explanation: Blocking recvfrom() waits until the datagram arrives and is copied into the application buffer.

questions.question: Which error is commonly returned in nonblocking I/O when no data is available?
questions.explanation: Nonblocking I/O returns EWOULDBLOCK when the requested operation cannot complete immediately.

questions.question: Which system call is used to enable nonblocking mode on a file descriptor?
questions.explanation: fcntl() is used to set the O_NONBLOCK flag on a file descriptor.

questions.question: Why can nonblocking I/O waste CPU time?
questions.option_a: A. Because it continuously allocates memory
questions.option_b: B. Because applications repeatedly poll descriptors
questions.option_d: D. Because it blocks the kernel
questions.explanation: Applications repeatedly call recvfrom() in polling loops, consuming CPU cycles.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of I/O multiplexing?
questions.option_b: B. Allows waiting on multiple descriptors simultaneously
questions.explanation: I/O multiplexing enables monitoring multiple descriptors for readiness.

questions.question: Which functions are commonly used for I/O multiplexing?
questions.explanation: select(), pselect(), and poll() are used for multiplexing I/O events.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of I/O multiplexing compared to blocking I/O?
questions.option_b: B. It requires two system calls
questions.option_c: C. It always wastes CPU time
questions.explanation: I/O multiplexing requires a select()/poll() call followed by the actual I/O call.

questions.question: Which signal is associated with signal-driven I/O?
questions.explanation: The kernel generates SIGIO when a descriptor becomes ready.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of signal-driven I/O?
questions.option_a: A. The process is not blocked waiting for data
questions.option_b: B. It avoids kernel calls completely
questions.explanation: Signal-driven I/O allows the process to continue executing until notified.

questions.question: What distinguishes asynchronous I/O from signal-driven I/O?
questions.option_a: A. Asynchronous I/O notifies when the entire operation completes
questions.option_c: C. Asynchronous I/O blocks the process
questions.option_d: D. Signal-driven I/O works only for files
questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O notifies the process after the complete operation, including data copying.

questions.question: According to POSIX definitions, which category includes blocking, nonblocking, multiplexing, and signal-driven I/O?
questions.explanation: These four models are considered synchronous because the process is involved during completion.

questions.question: Which I/O model does NOT block the requesting process?
questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O allows the process to continue executing while the operation completes.

questions.question: Which use case best fits I/O multiplexing?
questions.option_a: A. A client handling multiple sockets simultaneously
questions.option_b: B. A CPU performing arithmetic operations
questions.option_c: C. A process accessing only one descriptor
questions.option_d: D. A static file compression utility
questions.explanation: I/O multiplexing is ideal for applications handling many descriptors concurrently.

questions.question: What does select() return when the timeout expires before any descriptor becomes ready?
questions.explanation: select() returns 0 when the timeout expires without any ready descriptors.

questions.question: What additional feature does pselect() provide compared to select()?
questions.explanation: pselect() adds a signal mask parameter for atomic signal handling.

questions.question: Which structure is used by select() to specify timeout values?
questions.explanation: select() uses the timeval structure containing seconds and microseconds.

questions.question: What does FD_ZERO() do?
questions.option_b: B. Clears all bits in an fd_set
questions.option_c: C. Removes a descriptor from memory
questions.explanation: FD_ZERO() initializes the descriptor set by clearing all bits.

questions.question: Which macro checks whether a descriptor is part of an fd_set?
questions.explanation: FD_ISSET() checks whether the bit corresponding to a descriptor is set.

questions.question: If descriptors 2, 5, and 7 are monitored in select(), what should maxfdp1 be?
questions.explanation: maxfdp1 is the maximum descriptor plus one, so 7 + 1 = 8.

questions.question: Which condition makes a TCP socket readable?
questions.option_a: A. The send buffer is full
questions.option_b: B. Data has arrived in the receive buffer
questions.option_c: C. The socket is disconnected only
questions.option_d: D. The routing table is updated
questions.explanation: A socket becomes readable when data is available in the receive buffer.

questions.question: What happens when a TCP connection receives a FIN?
questions.option_b: B. The socket becomes unreadable permanently
questions.option_c: C. The socket becomes readable and read() returns 0
questions.explanation: Receiving a FIN causes read() to return 0, indicating EOF.

questions.question: What does fileno(FILE *stream) return?
questions.option_c: C. Integer descriptor associated with the stream
questions.explanation: fileno() extracts the file descriptor from a FILE stream.

questions.question: Why was the original str_cli() implementation problematic?
questions.option_b: B. It could block in fgets() and ignore socket events
questions.option_c: C. It used UDP instead of TCP
questions.explanation: The client could block waiting for user input while socket events were missed.

questions.question: What condition does FD_ISSET(sockfd, &rset) verify after select() returns?
questions.option_a: A. Whether the socket is writable
questions.option_b: B. Whether the socket is readable
questions.option_c: C. Whether the socket is closed permanently
questions.option_d: D. Whether the descriptor is invalid
questions.explanation: FD_ISSET checks if the socket is marked ready for reading.

questions.question: What is the main inefficiency of stop-and-wait mode?
questions.option_b: B. It waits one RTT for every request-response cycle
questions.explanation: Stop-and-wait sends one request and waits for a reply, reducing throughput.

questions.question: Why is shutdown() preferred over close() for partial TCP termination?
questions.option_d: D. close() only works for UDP
questions.explanation: shutdown() allows one direction of communication to close independently.

questions.question: Which shutdown() option closes only the write-half of a TCP connection?
questions.explanation: SHUT_WR closes the write-half while still allowing reads.

questions.question: What does SHUT_WR cause TCP to send?
questions.explanation: Closing the write-half causes a FIN segment to be transmitted.

questions.question: In the revised str_cli() using shutdown(), what happens after EOF is detected on standard input?
questions.option_a: A. The socket is fully closed immediately
questions.option_b: B. SHUT_WR is issued while reads continue
questions.option_d: D. The socket switches to UDP mode
questions.explanation: The client sends FIN but continues reading server responses.

questions.question: Why does a select()-based TCP echo server maintain a client[] array?
questions.option_b: B. To store connected socket descriptors
questions.explanation: The client array tracks active connected sockets.

questions.question: What does a value of -1 indicate in the client[] array?
questions.explanation: -1 marks unused entries in the client descriptor array.

questions.question: Why does the server copy allset into rset before calling select()?
questions.option_a: A. Because select() modifies descriptor sets
questions.option_b: B. Because allset cannot store descriptors
questions.option_c: C. Because rset is writable only
questions.option_d: D. Because allset is temporary memory
questions.explanation: select() changes descriptor sets to indicate ready descriptors.

questions.question: What does the server do when Readline() returns 0 for a client socket?
questions.option_b: B. Closes the connection and removes the descriptor
questions.explanation: A return value of 0 indicates the client closed the connection.

questions.question: Which structure is used by poll() to monitor descriptors?
questions.explanation: poll() uses an array of pollfd structures.

questions.question: Which field in struct pollfd specifies the events being monitored?
questions.explanation: The events field defines the conditions of interest.

questions.question: What does POLLIN indicate in poll()?
questions.explanation: POLLIN indicates readable data is available.

questions.question: What happens if timeout is set to 0 in poll()?
questions.explanation: A timeout of 0 causes immediate return after checking descriptors.

questions.question: What does INFTIM mean in poll()?
questions.explanation: INFTIM causes poll() to block indefinitely.

questions.question: Why can a blocking server be vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks?
questions.option_a: A. Because attackers can monopolize blocking reads
questions.explanation: A malicious client can keep the server blocked waiting for more data.

questions.question: Which technique can help mitigate denial-of-service attacks caused by blocking reads?
questions.explanation: Nonblocking I/O prevents a single client from indefinitely blocking the server.

questions.question: What is deadlock in network systems?
questions.option_b: B. Permanent waiting between communicating parties
questions.explanation: Deadlock occurs when entities wait forever for events that never occur.

questions.question: How does starvation differ from deadlock?
questions.option_a: A. Starvation means some clients never receive service
questions.option_b: B. Starvation always crashes the kernel
questions.option_d: D. Starvation only occurs in UDP
questions.explanation: Starvation occurs when some clients are unfairly denied service.

questions.question: A client using blocking fgets() never notices that the server process terminated. Which design solves this issue?
questions.option_b: B. Using I/O multiplexing with select()
questions.explanation: select() allows simultaneous monitoring of stdin and sockets.

questions.question: Why is asynchronous I/O considered more scalable than polling-based nonblocking I/O?
questions.option_a: A. Because it eliminates repeated readiness checks
questions.option_c: C. Because it requires no kernel interaction
questions.option_d: D. Because it uses synchronous blocking
questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O avoids constant polling loops that waste CPU cycles.

questions.question: A TCP socket monitored by select() receives an RST from the peer. What is the likely read() result?
questions.explanation: RST indicates a reset connection, causing read() to return an error.

questions.question: Why is stop-and-wait mode inefficient on high-latency networks?
questions.option_a: A. Because RTT delays every transaction
questions.option_b: B. Because FIN packets are duplicated
questions.explanation: Every request waits an RTT before continuing, limiting throughput.

questions.question: In poll(), what happens if fd is set to a negative value?
questions.option_a: A. The descriptor is automatically reopened
questions.explanation: Negative descriptors are ignored by poll().

questions.question: Why might poll() be preferred over select() in large systems?
questions.option_a: A. poll() avoids fixed descriptor bitmaps
questions.option_b: B. poll() only works for UDP
questions.explanation: poll() uses arrays rather than fixed-size descriptor sets.

questions.question: What is the purpose of low-water marks in socket buffers?
questions.option_a: A. To control minimum data availability thresholds
questions.explanation: Low-water marks define how much data must be available before readiness.

questions.question: A server handles all clients using one blocking read() loop. One client stops sending data after one byte. What is the MOST likely result?
questions.option_a: A. The server continues serving all clients normally
questions.option_b: B. The server blocks waiting for that client
questions.option_c: C. The kernel automatically disconnects the client
questions.option_d: D. The server switches to asynchronous mode
questions.explanation: Blocking reads can allow one malicious client to stall the server.

questions.question: What is the purpose of FD_CLR()?
questions.option_b: B. To clear a descriptor bit from an fd_set
questions.explanation: FD_CLR removes a descriptor from the monitored set.

questions.question: Which poll() event indicates a hang-up occurred?
questions.explanation: POLLHUP signals that a hang-up occurred on the descriptor.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the listening socket in a select()-based TCP server?
questions.explanation: The listening socket becomes readable when new connections are pending.

questions.question: Why must applications reinitialize descriptor sets before each select() call?
questions.option_a: A. Because select() modifies the sets
questions.option_d: D. Because Linux deletes descriptors after reads
questions.explanation: select() changes the sets to indicate readiness, so they must be rebuilt.

questions.question: A server uses shutdown(sockfd, SHUT_WR). Which behavior is correct afterward?
questions.option_a: A. Both reads and writes are disabled
questions.option_b: B. Writes stop, but reads can continue
questions.option_c: C. Reads stop, but writes continue
questions.option_d: D. The socket descriptor becomes invalid immediately
questions.explanation: SHUT_WR closes only the write-half while allowing reads.

questions.question: Which statement best describes asynchronous I/O notifications?
questions.option_b: B. The kernel notifies after the full operation completes
questions.option_c: C. The process blocks in recvfrom()
questions.option_d: D. Notifications occur before data arrival
questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O completion notifications occur after the entire operation finishes.

questions.question: Why is deadlock detection difficult in distributed systems?
questions.option_a: A. Because resources and dependencies are distributed
questions.explanation: Distributed dependencies make deadlock analysis complex.
